title: Keeping ties
hook: a relative gone quiet, and a promise about provision and life

segments.voice: Yesterday, justice, and your line: nearest to taqwa. Did you find a small scale and keep your thumb off it? Today, the people none of us chose. Day one thousand three hundred thirteen.

Somewhere in a phone there's a family name with no messages since last year. An aunt. A cousin. A brother, after something nobody brings up at dinner. Families drift without anyone deciding to let them. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, attaches a promise to exactly those names. In paraphrase: whoever would like his provision to be widened and his life to be lengthened, let him keep his ties of kinship. Blessing in life, tied to a phone call. Today's word is the tie itself.
screen: `A NAME WITH NO MESSAGES.` → `FAMILIES DRIFT.` → `WIDER PROVISION, LONGER LIFE.`

segments.voice: The phrase is silat al-rahim. Silah is a connection, a joining. Rahim is the womb, and through it everyone you're related to by birth. The opening verse of surah al-Nisa asks people, in paraphrase, to be mindful of Allah, and of the wombs, the kinship by which they ask things of one another. Second, the name inside the word. In Bukhari, the Prophet says, in paraphrase: the rahim is a branch from al-Rahman, the Most Merciful. Whoever keeps it joined, Allah keeps joined to him; whoever cuts it, Allah cuts off. The word for family and the name of mercy share their letters, and the hadith turns that into a bond. Third, the hard part, also in Bukhari. In paraphrase: the one who keeps ties isn't the one who simply repays in kind. The one who keeps ties is the one who, when the tie has been cut, joins it again. Not the relative who calls back. The one who calls first, after the silence. And in Sahih Muslim, a man brings the Prophet his complaint. I keep ties with my relatives, and they cut me. I'm good to them, and they're bad to me. The answer, in paraphrase: if it's as you say, it's as if you're feeding them hot ashes, and a helper from Allah stays with you as long as you keep on. Fourth, a caution. Keeping ties doesn't require pretending harm never happened. What a tie looks like with a truly harmful relative is a question to bring to a scholar you trust. But the default the hadith sets is the open line.
screen: `SILAH: A JOINING. RAHIM: THE WOMB.` · `A BRANCH FROM AL-RAHMAN.` · `REJOIN WHAT WAS CUT.` · `HOT ASHES, AND A HELPER.`

segments.voice: The practice: contact a relative. Not yet. First, settle, and breathe. Let one relative come to mind, someone you've let drift. Not the hardest one. Just one. See their face. Remember one good thing about them: a meal, a joke, a ride somewhere years ago. Then decide what you'll send after the bell. A few words. A voice note. An old photo. Keep it small enough that you'll actually do it. If you pray, you can make du'a for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Silat al-rahim. Keeping the ties of kinship, the rahim a hadith calls a branch from al-Rahman: joined again, even when someone else cut it. Today's word.

Your line: keep the ties. Today, send that one message to that one relative, and don't stop to work out who was supposed to call last. Tomorrow, loving for others. Day one thousand three hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Muslims treat silat al-rahim, keeping ties with relatives, as a religious duty: visiting, calling, helping and greeting family, and reaching out again after a falling-out.

trapdoor: what you thought: family ties means getting along at holidays.
what it means: silat al-rahim is actively keeping kinship joined, even reaching first across a silence.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 5988 calls the rahim a branch from al-Rahman, and 5991 defines the tie-keeper as the one who rejoins what was cut.

Editor: cut the unsourced claim that scholars allow ties with a harmful relative to shrink to 'a greeting'; teach now points such cases to a trusted scholar. Hook's 'a lot of phones' (a sweeping claim) changed to 'a phone'.
'The word for family and the name of mercy share their letters': rahim and al-Rahman share the root r-h-m; the hadith itself makes the link. Confirm phrasing.
